analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover hospital stays, breast reconstruction, and second opinions after breast cancer surgery.
analysis.headline: Despite 26 bipartisan cosponsors and a Senate hearing, the bill never left the Finance Committee and died without a vote when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employer health plans, health insurers, and individual-market coverage to pay for inpatient care after breast cancer surgery for as long as the patient's doctor says is medically appropriate, for all stages of breast reconstruction, and for second opinions from cancer specialists. It also barred plans from penalizing doctors who provide this care or from rewarding doctors for cutting hospital stays short. The requirements would have reached employer plans through three federal laws at once, so most insured women would have been covered.
analysis.who_benefits: Women going through breast cancer treatment who have coverage through an employer plan or the individual market. They would no longer face "drive-through" mastectomies limited to 23 hours or uncovered, out-of-pocket costs for reconstructive surgery and symmetry surgery on the other breast, and they could get a specialist second opinion to confirm or rule out a cancer diagnosis at in-network cost even from a doctor outside the plan. Plans could not rewrite a patient's coverage because she declined some of the required benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Breast cancer patients in group and individual plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover inpatient care after a mastectomy, lumpectomy, or lymph node dissection for as long as the attending physician and the patient jointly determine is medically appropriate — with the patient and doctor still free to choose a shorter stay.
Requires coverage of all stages of reconstruction of the breast on which the mastectomy was performed, plus surgery and reconstruction of the other breast to produce a symmetrical appearance.

Requires full coverage of second-opinion consultations with cancer specialists (pathology, radiology, oncology) to confirm or refute a diagnosis, and if network specialists are not sufficiently available, coverage of any specialist the attending physician picks at no extra cost to the patient.

Bars plans from cutting a doctor's reimbursement for providing this care, from paying doctors incentives to keep mastectomy stays short or to limit second-opinion referrals, and from changing a patient's coverage terms because she asked for less than the minimum benefits.
Extends the same protections to the individual insurance market and to employer plans through the tax code, reaching most kinds of private coverage rather than only some.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers whose plans provide medical and surgical benefits would bear the added cost of longer hospital stays, reconstruction surgery, and second opinions — costs that would ultimately flow into premiums paid by all enrollees. Plans also bear the administrative cost of mailing required notices to participants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers offering coverage

drawbacks.text: The required benefits add real costs: longer hospital stays, multi-stage reconstruction surgery, and out-of-network second opinions would be paid by insurers and employers and ultimately built into premiums for every enrollee in a plan, not just those facing breast cancer.

The reconstruction guarantee is written as consistent with any fee schedule the plan already has, which leaves insurers room to set the rates and constrain what doctors are paid for the newly required surgery.

A federal mandate of this kind overrides plan design choices that some plans had made to control costs, and grandfathered collective bargaining plans were given until their contracts expired rather than immediate coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were concrete and targeted at a moment — breast cancer surgery — when patients historically had little leverage against plan rules limiting hospital time or denying reconstruction. The costs are real but diffuse: higher premiums spread across millions of enrollees, with doctor-patient judgment (not a fixed federal number) setting the stay length, which blunts the "one-size-fits-all" objection. The serious failure here is not the bill's design but its fate: with 26 cosponsors from both parties and a committee hearing on the record, it was never given a vote, so the merits were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in January 1997, got one subcommittee hearing that November, and was never reported out or voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator D'Amato introduced the bill on January 30, 1997 with 16 original cosponsors from both parties, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The referral was the only committee step for ten months; the sole additional action was a Health Care Subcommittee hearing on November 5, 1997, printed as S.Hrg. 105-917.

The bill's cosponsor list grew to 26 — 10 Republicans and 16 Democrats — and D'Amato gave new introductory remarks on the floor on May 14, 1998, but the committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee with no vote ever taken in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers offering medical coverage are better off because the bill died: they never had to cover extended post-surgical stays, reconstruction, or guaranteed second opinions. Women facing breast cancer surgery got none of the federal protections this bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Alfonse D'Amato
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor at introduction (January 1997) and again in May 1998.

for.name: 10 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Olympia Snowe, Pete Domenici, Lauch Faircloth, Frank Murkowski, Orrin Hatch, Judd Gregg, Bob Smith, and Wendell Ford.

for.name: 16 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Dianne Feinstein, Ernest Hollings, Daniel Patrick Moynihan, Carol Moseley-Braun, Joseph Biden, Daniel Inouye, Christopher Dodd, and Bob Kerrey.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman William V. Roth Jr. (R-DE)
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the committee for two years; after a single subcommittee hearing in November 1997, no markup was scheduled and the bill was never reported to the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the 17 original cosponsors split roughly evenly between Republicans and Democrats, and the final roster of 26 included 10 Republicans and 16 Democrats; no senator is on record against it because no vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill mandates coverage of extended post-surgical stays, full reconstruction, and second opinions across group and individual markets, directly expanding what insurers must pay for. Insurers also could no longer use doctor bonuses to shorten stays or limit referrals, removing a cost-control lever.

By amending ERISA and the tax code, the bill reaches self-insured employer plans, so large employers would absorb the added benefit costs in plan years beginning after enactment (with grandfathered union contracts deferred until they expire).

The inpatient requirement guarantees hospital revenue for stays after mastectomy, lumpectomy, and lymph node dissection whenever the physician and patient judge it appropriate. Here hospital revenue and patient interests point the same way.

Coverage of all stages of breast reconstruction and symmetry surgery on the other breast creates guaranteed payment for services many plans previously excluded. The catch is that payment must fit the plan's existing fee schedule.
